Fitting a VAR and choosing the lag order¶

Back to Vector Autoregressions and Cointegration

A vector autoregression (VAR) models several series together, each as a linear function of the past values of all of them:

y_t = c + A₁ y_{t−1} + … + A_p y_{t−p} + e_t, Cov(e_t) = Σ.

Where a univariate AR model says “this series depends on its own past”, a VAR also says “and on the past of the others”. The cross-coefficients are the point: a VAR can describe interest rates that follow output, or two prices that pull each other. Every equation has the same regressors, so the Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate is just least squares, equation by equation, and the covariance of the errors Σ carries the contemporaneous relation between the series.

Var::fit_mle(y, VarOptions) takes y as an n × k matrix, one column per series, and returns a VarFit with the constant (length k), ar (a p × k × k array), the error covariance (k × k) and the sample_size = n − p of rows used. This page shows how to read the fit, choose the order p, and check that the cross-effects earn their parameters.

The layout of ar. ar[l][j][i] is the coefficient of series j at lag l + 1 in the equation of series i. So row j of each lag matrix lists the effect of series j on all series. The same convention (shock index first, response index last) is used by the impulse responses on the next page.

The three programs use a simulated two-series system: a_t = 0.5 a_{t−1} + 0.2 b_{t−1} + e_{a,t} and b_t = 0.1 a_{t−1} + 0.6 b_{t−1} + e_{b,t}, where the two shocks are correlated. A helper builds the generating model as a VarFit filled in by hand; simulate then draws data from it.

Choosing the lag order¶

How many lags? The same trade-off as for ARIMA (Choosing the orders): more lags always fit the sample better, so a criterion charges for the parameters. A VAR(p) in k series has k (k p + 1) coefficients (the constant and the p matrices of size k × k in each equation) and k(k+1)/2 more in Σ, which are the same for every p and cancel in a comparison. Smaller is better for Akaike’s criterion −2 loglik + 2m and for Schwarz’s −2 loglik + m log n. Note that models with different p must be compared on the same observations; the fit uses n − p rows, so the log-likelihoods are on slightly different samples, which is a small effect that this page ignores.

The program fits p = 1…4 to two datasets, one generated by a VAR(1) and one by a VAR(2), and reports which order each criterion selects.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace ts = pluss::subsp::stats::ts;
using pluss::Series;

ts::VarFit make_truth(int lags, const pluss::Config& cfg) {
  ts::VarFit t;
  t.lag_order = lags;
  t.constant = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.0}, cfg);
  if (lags == 1) {
    t.ar = pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.1, 0.2, 0.6}, {1, 2, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  } else {  // a second lag on top of the first
    t.ar = pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.1, 0.2, 0.6, -0.3, 0.0, 0.0, -0.2}, {2, 2, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  }
  t.covariance = pluss::make_series({0.08, 0.04, 0.04, 0.10}, {2, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  return t;
}

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  for (int true_lags : {1, 2}) {
    const Series y = make_truth(true_lags, f64).simulate(400, f64, /*seed=*/3);
    std::cout << "data generated by a VAR(" << true_lags << ")\n";
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(1) << std::setw(6) << "lags" << std::setw(12) << "loglik" << std::setw(12) << "Akaike" << std::setw(12) << "Schwarz" << "\n";
    double best_a = 1e300, best_b = 1e300;
    int pa = 0, pb = 0;
    for (int p = 1; p <= 4; ++p) {
      ts::VarOptions o;
      o.lag_order = p;
      const auto fit = ts::Var::fit_mle(y, o, f64);
      const double ll = fit.loglik(y), m = 2.0 * (2.0 * p + 1.0);
      const double aic = -2 * ll + 2 * m, bic = -2 * ll + m * std::log(static_cast<double>(fit.sample_size));
      std::cout << std::setw(6) << p << std::setw(12) << ll << std::setw(12) << aic << std::setw(12) << bic << "\n";
      if (aic < best_a) { best_a = aic; pa = p; }
      if (bic < best_b) { best_b = bic; pb = p; }
    }
    std::cout << "selected: Akaike " << pa << ", Schwarz " << pb << "\n\n";
  }
}

Output

data generated by a VAR(1)
  lags      loglik      Akaike     Schwarz
     1      -129.0       270.0       293.9
     2      -127.4       274.8       314.7
     3      -124.5       277.0       332.8
     4      -122.3       280.5       352.2
selected: Akaike 1, Schwarz 1

data generated by a VAR(2)
  lags      loglik      Akaike     Schwarz
     1      -149.7       311.5       335.4
     2      -126.6       273.1       313.0
     3      -124.5       277.0       332.7
     4      -121.9       279.9       351.5
selected: Akaike 2, Schwarz 2

Both criteria recover the true order in both datasets when the signal is this clear. The usual caveats apply: with a short sample or weak cross-effects, Akaike’s criterion tends to choose more lags than Schwarz’s, and the right order is the smallest one whose residuals are clean. A VAR also uses up parameters quickly: ten series with four lags have about 400 coefficients, which is why large systems are restricted or regularised (VarOptions::ridge).

Reading the fit¶

The second program fits the VAR(1) and prints everything the fit holds beside the generating values, then forecasts three steps ahead. Look at the layout: ar row 0 is the effect of series 0 on series 0 then series 1, row 1 the effect of series 1 on each.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>


namespace ts = pluss::subsp::stats::ts;
using pluss::Series;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(3));
  ts::VarFit truth;
  truth.lag_order = 1;
  truth.constant = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.0}, f64);
  truth.ar = pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.1, 0.2, 0.6}, {1, 2, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  truth.covariance = pluss::make_series({0.08, 0.04, 0.04, 0.10}, {2, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  const Series y = truth.simulate(400, f64, /*seed=*/3);

  const auto fit = ts::Var::fit_mle(y, {}, f64);
  out.writeln("constant              ", fit.constant.host<double>(), "(true 0, 0)");
  out.writeln("A1 row 0: series 0 feeds", fit.ar.select(0, 0).select(0, 0).host<double>(), "(true 0.5, 0.1)");
  out.writeln("A1 row 1: series 1 feeds", fit.ar.select(0, 0).select(0, 1).host<double>(), "(true 0.2, 0.6)");
  out.writeln("covariance row 0      ", fit.covariance.select(0, 0).host<double>(), "(true 0.08, 0.04)");
  out.writeln("covariance row 1      ", fit.covariance.select(0, 1).host<double>(), "(true 0.04, 0.10)");
  out.writeln("sample size", fit.sample_size);
  out.writeln("forecasts, three steps ahead (rows are steps)");
  const auto f = fit.forecast(3, y, f64);
  for (int h = 0; h < 3; ++h) out.writeln("  step", h + 1, f.select(0, h).host<double>());
}

Output

constant               [0.006, 0.004] (true 0, 0)
A1 row 0: series 0 feeds [0.560, 0.175] (true 0.5, 0.1)
A1 row 1: series 1 feeds [0.186, 0.585] (true 0.2, 0.6)
covariance row 0       [0.082, 0.040] (true 0.08, 0.04)
covariance row 1       [0.040, 0.099] (true 0.04, 0.10)
sample size 399
forecasts, three steps ahead (rows are steps)
  step 1 [-0.014, -0.159]
  step 2 [-0.032, -0.092]
  step 3 [-0.030, -0.056]

The coefficients are within sampling error of the truth (for instance 0.560 and 0.585 against 0.5 and 0.6 on the own-lag diagonal), and the cross-effects are the ones to look at: 0.186 (series 1 feeding series 0, true 0.2) and 0.175 (series 0 feeding series 1, true 0.1). The covariance is the maximum-likelihood estimate (the residual cross-products divided by the number of rows used), and its off-diagonal 0.040 is the contemporaneous relation of the two shocks. The forecasts start from the last observation and decay towards the means as in a univariate AR; each row is one step and each column one series.

Do the cross-effects help?¶

The point of a VAR over separate AR models is the cross-effects. The program tests whether they pay in forecasting: it fits both models on the first 300 observations, then makes one-step forecasts for each of the remaining 100 observations (using the data up to each date) and compares the root mean squared error for each series, the VAR against an AR(1) fitted to the series alone.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace ts = pluss::subsp::stats::ts;
using pluss::Series;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  ts::VarFit truth;
  truth.lag_order = 1;
  truth.constant = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.0}, f64);
  truth.ar = pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.1, 0.2, 0.6}, {1, 2, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  truth.covariance = pluss::make_series({0.08, 0.04, 0.04, 0.10}, {2, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  const int n = 400, train = 300;
  const Series y = truth.simulate(n, f64, /*seed=*/3);
  const auto all = y.host<double>();  // row t: series 0 at 2t, series 1 at 2t + 1

  auto prefix = [&](int rows) { return pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>(all.begin(), all.begin() + 2 * rows), {rows, 2}).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64); };
  auto column = [&](int rows, int j) {
    std::vector<double> c(rows);
    for (int t = 0; t < rows; ++t) c[t] = all[2 * t + j];
    return pluss::make_series(c, f64);
  };

  const auto var = ts::Var::fit_mle(prefix(train), {}, f64);
  ts::ArimaOptions ao;
  ao.ar_order = 1;
  const auto ar0 = ts::Arima::fit_mle(column(train, 0), ao, f64);
  const auto ar1 = ts::Arima::fit_mle(column(train, 1), ao, f64);

  double se_var[2] = {0, 0}, se_ar[2] = {0, 0};
  for (int t = train; t < n; ++t) {
    const auto fv = var.forecast(1, prefix(t), f64).host<double>();
    const double fa[2] = {ar0.forecast(1, column(t, 0), f64).host<double>()[0], ar1.forecast(1, column(t, 1), f64).host<double>()[0]};
    for (int j = 0; j < 2; ++j) {
      const double actual = all[2 * t + j];
      se_var[j] += (actual - fv[j]) * (actual - fv[j]);
      se_ar[j] += (actual - fa[j]) * (actual - fa[j]);
    }
  }
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
  std::cout << std::left << std::setw(10) << "series" << std::right << std::setw(14) << "VAR(1) RMSE" << std::setw(16) << "own AR(1) RMSE" << "\n";
  for (int j = 0; j < 2; ++j)
    std::cout << std::left << std::setw(10) << j << std::right << std::setw(14) << std::sqrt(se_var[j] / (n - train)) << std::setw(16) << std::sqrt(se_ar[j] / (n - train)) << "\n";
}

Output

series       VAR(1) RMSE  own AR(1) RMSE
0                 0.3079          0.3184
1                 0.3360          0.3446

The VAR has the lower error for both series, by about 3% (0.308 against 0.318 for series 0, 0.336 against 0.345 for series 1). The gain is small because the cross-effects are small (0.1 and 0.2 against own-lag coefficients of 0.5 and 0.6); a stronger coupling gives a larger gain, and no coupling gives none. This is the out-of-sample version of the question a Granger test answers in sample (Granger tests). If the gain is zero for every series, the system is better described by separate models, which have far fewer parameters.

Decisions and pitfalls¶

  • Stationary series only, in levels. A VAR in levels assumes stationarity. If the series have unit roots, difference them or test for cointegration first (The rank of a cointegrated system).

  • Choose p with a criterion and check the residuals. Residual autocorrelation of any series means more lags are needed.

  • Mind the parameter count. It grows with k² p; for many series use ridge shrinkage or restrict the system.

  • Order is irrelevant for fitting but matters later. The orthogonalised impulse responses depend on the ordering of the columns (next page).

  • Compare on equal footing. Criteria for different p use slightly different samples; keep n large relative to p.
